title: Day 34 · Week 4, Day 6 — Myths: you can't know this early, one glass of wine is fine, and pregnancy tests get it wrong all the time
summary: The first Myths episode, on the last day of Week 4. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 9 — 1.5–2.5 mm, a sesame seed with a neural groove, one to three somite pairs, a cardiogenic region and the first blood islands on the yolk sac. Myth one, 'you can't really know this early': the sensitive home tests detect 97% of pregnancies on the day of the missed period (the less sensitive ones 54–67%), a positive is almost certainly correct — but what you can't know is how it ends: Wilcox 1988 found 22% of implanted pregnancies lost before they could be recognised and 31% in all, and a scan at Day 34 would likely show an empty uterus (sac threshold hCG ~390, discriminatory ~3,510). Myth two, 'one glass is fine': every guideline says none; the cohorts at ≤2 drinks a week can't find an effect on IQ or birthweight (Henderson 2007, 46 studies; Mamluk 2017, SGA OR 1.08; Danish cohorts 2012, with the confounding tell), pooled analyses find small behaviour effects (Flak 2014; ABCD 2020), and the miscarriage data do not look null — OR 1.19 in 231,808 women, +6% per weekly drink, and +8% per week of drinking from week 5 in a 5,353-woman cohort, independent of amount. Why the guidelines say none anyway, what to say about drinking before the test (UK CMOs: unlikely the baby has been affected), and why the father's drinking is most of the context. Myth three, 'tests get it wrong': the real false positives (hCG trigger shots, a recent pregnancy, pituitary hCG with age, evaporation lines read late) and false negatives (too early, dilute urine, the beta-core-fragment hook effect after five weeks, and strips that 30–40% of women misread).
action: Tonight, ten minutes. Put the remaining pregnancy tests in a drawer — after a positive on or after Day 28 the next useful test is the scan. Settle the alcohol rule for the next 35 weeks together; the simplest version the evidence has no argument with is that you drink what she drinks. Move the bottles out of the kitchen and agree the one sentence for when someone pours: 'The guideline is none, so we're doing none' — you say it, so she doesn't have to. If there was drinking before the test, note roughly how much and when for the first visit, then let it go.
